bib.title: CoAct-1: Computer-using Multi-Agent System with Coding Actions

legacy_report:
COVERAGE: all 17 of 17 pages read (59,111 chars), including the appendices. No extraction faults. The text contains no embedded instructions. The prompt tables in Appendix C are the paper's own agent prompts, not directed at me.

SOURCE: "CoAct-1: Computer-using Multi-agent System with Coding Actions". Linxin Song (USC, work done as a Salesforce intern), Yutong Dai, Viraj Prabhu, Jieyu Zhang (UW), Taiwei Shi, Li Li, Junnan Li, Silvio Savarese, Zeyuan Chen, Jieyu Zhao, Ran Xu, Caiming Xiong (Salesforce AI Research). The PDF header reads "Published as a conference paper at ICLR 2026"; arXiv 2508.03923 v3, 20 Feb 2026. Code: github.com/SalesforceAIResearch/CoAct-1.

CORE CLAIM: A GUI-only computer-use agent is brittle and slow. An Orchestrator that delegates each subtask to either a GUI Operator or a Programmer (which writes Python/Bash) beats GUI-only systems on OSWorld and WindowsAgentArena. The gain comes from a wider action space (code as an action), not from a new multi-agent topology.

HEADLINE NUMBERS
Setup for all of them:
- Orchestrator is o3-2025-04-16, Programmer is o4-mini, GUI Operator is OpenAI computer-use-preview, summarizer is o4-mini. Built on AG2.
- Caps: Programmer 20 rounds, GUI Operator 25 steps, Orchestrator 15 rounds, so at most 375 interactions. Every task stopped before 150 steps.
- OSWorld is 369 tasks, WindowsAgentArena is 154. Scoring is the benchmark's rule-based evaluators.
- No run count, seeds, variance, confidence intervals or cost (dollars or tokens) are reported.

- OSWorld: 60.76% at the 150-step limit. At 100 steps it is 59.93%. Agent S2.5 w/ o3 gets 55.98% and GTA-1 w/ o3 gets 53.07%, both at 100 steps.
- At 15 steps CoAct-1 scores 39.81%, below Jedi-7B w/ o3 (42.37%). At 50 steps it scores 56.38%, ahead of Agent S2.5 (54.21%).
- WindowsAgentArena: 52.5% at 100 steps, 43.5% at 50 and 21.4% at 15. Agent S2 gets 29.8%.
- Average steps on solved tasks (100-step budget): CoAct-1 10.15, GTA-1 15.22, UI-TARS 14.90, OpenAI CUA 4o 6.14. CUA 4o is cheaper per solved task but scores 31.4% against 59.93%.

ABLATIONS (OSWorld, Tables 3 and 4)
- Role of the model (Table 3), with CUA 4o as GUI Operator in every row:

| Orchestrator | Programmer | OSWorld |
|---|---|---|
| o4-mini | o4-mini | 43.43 |
| o3 | o3 | 58.72 |
| o3 | o4-mini | 60.76 |

  The authors read this as "strategically allocating powerful models to roles with high reasoning demands". It is a single run each, so the 2-point gap between the last two rows is not shown to be reliable.
- Hybrid against single modality (Table 4):

| Setup | Success | Avg steps |
|---|---|---|
| Programmer only | 35.73% | 1.14 |
| GUI Operator only | 50.68% | 11.20 |
| Both | 60.76% | 10.15 |

  The "avg steps" column is steps per success. The Programmer-only figure is therefore not comparable, since it solves only the easy tasks.
- There is no ablation of the summariser, memory isolation or the Orchestrator itself (for example, a single agent given both tools).

KEY QUOTES
- p5: "To ensure modularity and focus, these memories are isolated; the agents do not share their conversational histories directly. Furthermore, once an executor completes its subtask and reports back to the Orchestrator, its working memory is cleared."
- p5: "this detailed history is processed by a dedicated summarizer model. This model condenses the entire interaction into a concise summary ... This summary, along with the final screenshot ... is then returned to the Orchestrator."
- p13-14: "only the final state of the OS will be returned to the orchestrator after the GUI operator completes the task. This issue yields the final error if the GUI Operator makes some middle-state errors and the new operation covers them."
- p13: "the GUI Operator has a significant hallucination rate when performing self-checks, while the Programmer's file modifications do not reflect in the OS" (so the Orchestrator verifies independently).

LIMITS
- It is not a controlled test of multi-agent against single-agent. The ablation compares action modalities, not topologies, so it does not show that the Orchestrator and executor split itself helps. The context-firewall design (isolated executor memory, summary handoff) is described but never ablated.
- Benchmark and model scope. Only OpenAI models were used. The authors had no GPU budget to test open GUI models. There is no cost or latency figure, and every number comes from one run on one benchmark family.
- The authors list four failure types (Appendix D):
  - High-level queries needing intent inference.
  - Ambiguous queries. The Programmer edited workspace settings instead of user settings.
  - Reflection errors, where only the final state is returned to the Orchestrator, so intermediate GUI mistakes are hidden.
  - Hallucination. The Orchestrator plans against unseen content, and the GUI Operator claims to have finished.
- The mitigation is prompt-based: more frequent verification and cross-checking between the two executors. Its effect is not measured.
- Summariser fidelity is not measured, and the summary is lossy by design.
- The model names (o3, o4-mini, CUA preview) and the leaderboard position have dated.

BUILDS ON
- AutoGen (Wu et al. 2023), through the AG2 framework.
- The planner-grounder line: Agent S/S2/S2.5 (Agashe 2024, 2025), GTA-1 (Yang 2025), Jedi (Xie 2025).
- Benchmarks: OSWorld (Xie 2024) and WindowsAgentArena (Bonatti 2024).
- Hybrid tool-or-API agents: UFO-2, PyVision, Beyond Browsing (Song 2025b), ALITA.

FIT TO NOTE 07
Weak to moderate, and only as a supporting citation. It gives one evidence point for:
- hierarchical orchestrator with specialist executors;
- an isolated executor context cleared after each subtask, with a summary handoff;
- a strong model for the planner and a cheaper one for the executor (Table 3).

It also gives a concrete failure mode for handoff design: the executor's final-state-only report hides intermediate errors, and a summariser can lose them. It does not evidence the context-firewall benefit or the "when not to go multi-agent" point. Its main thesis is action-space design, so note 03 (tool design) fits better for the code-as-action claim. Note 05 (verification) fits for the self-check hallucination and the independent Orchestrator re-check.

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Figure 1 or 2 on p3-4 (the Orchestrator, Programmer and GUI Operator workflow), where Figure 2 is captioned "Illustration of CoAct-1 workflow. Given a user task, Orchestrator can choose either to call Programmer or GUI Operator to solve a subtask." The workflow diagrams are image-only, so I could not inspect them from the text extraction. Figure 3d (p8, pass/fail by total steps) is an alternative.
